claim: Echolocating bats have excellent spatial memory.
source: Echolocating bats have excellent spatial memory (Barchi et al., 2013; Holland, 2007; Geva-Sagiv et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to three published studies

claim: Echolocating bats are able to navigate to salient locations like roosts, foraging grounds and drinking places.
source: are able to navigate to salient locations like roosts, foraging grounds and drinking places (Schnitzler et al., 2003)

claim: Long distance navigation and migration in Phyllostomus hastatus and Rousettus aegyptiacus are supported mainly by visual cues.
source: Experimental results obtained using both Phyllostomus hastatus and Rousettus aegyptiacus suggest that long distance navigation and migration seem to be supported mainly by visual cues (Tsoar et al., 2011; Holland, 2007)

claim: When displaced by less than about 15 km, both Myotis spp. and Phyllostomus hastatus deprived of sight have been found to successfully return to their roost.

claim: Navigation in bats can be supported by echolocation as well as vision.
source: This shows that navigation in bats can be supported by echolocation as well as vision.

claim: Navigating and route-following require animals to recognize places.
source: Navigating and route-following require animals to recognize places (Franz and Mallot, 2000)

claim: It is largely unknown how bats recognize places using echolocation.
source: Currently, it is largely unknown how bats recognize places using echolocation (Schnitzler et al., 2003)

claim: The position, shape, size and texture of objects are all encoded in the binaural spectra of the echoes.
source: Under favourable conditions, extracting a description of a set of localized objects from the echoes is possible as the position, shape, size and texture of objects are all encoded in the binaural spectra of the echoes, e.g. (Reijniers et al., 2010; Schmidt, 1988; Von Helversen and Von Helversen, 2003; Peremans et al., 2012; Wotton and Simmons, 2000; Simon et al., 2011; Genzel and Wiegrebe, 2013)

claim: Low signal-to-noise ratio obscures echo spectra.
source: Low signal-to-noise ratio obscures echo spectra (Reijniers et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Sonar has a limited field of view compared to vision.
source: compared to vision, sonar has a limited field of view (Surlykke et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Sonar has a low update rate.
source: a low update rate (Kleeman and Kuc, 2008; Peremans et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Sonar has a limited range.
source: a limited range (Stilz and Schnitzler, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Wiegrebe and Schmidt (1996) observed a temporal integration constant of about 200 μs in Megaderma lyra.
source: In a psychophysical experiment, Wiegrebe and Schmidt (1996) observed a temporal integration constant of about 200 μs in Megaderma lyra.

source: Simmons and colleagues (Simmons et al., 1989) derived an integration constant of about 200–400 μs for the bat Eptesicus fuscus.

claim: At 7.8 meters distance, a system with a functional beamwidth of 60 degrees integrates echoes from a volume of about 2 m³.
source: At the same distance, a system with a functional beamwidth of 60 degrees integrates echoes from a volume of about 2 m3.

claim: Non-simultaneous masking effects have been found to extend for substantially longer intervals than the integration time in both bats and humans.
source: Indeed, non-simultaneous masking effects have been found to extend for substantially longer intervals than the integration time (both in bats and humans [Moore, 2012])
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: Geberl (2013) found non-simultaneous masking in Phyllostomus discolor for temporal separation between echoes up to 6 ms.
source: For example, Geberl (2013) found non-simultaneous masking in Phyllostomus discolor for temporal separation between echoes up to 6 ms.

claim: Grunwald et al. (2004) reported that bats can discriminate between echoes with different impulse response statistics.
source: Grunwald et al. (2004) reported that bats can discriminate between echoes with different impulse response statistics.
evidence: Supported by citation to specific study

claim: The auditory periphery of the bat retains sufficient information to allow responding to the stochastic properties of the underlying impulse responses.
source: This shows that the auditory periphery of the bat retains sufficient information to allow responding to the stochastic properties of the underlying impulse responses.
evidence: Inferred from the Grunwald et al. (2004) findings

claim: Bats can discriminate between echoes with different impulse response statistics does not necessarily imply that bats can reconstruct the impulse response from the echoes.
source: However, this does not necessarily imply that bats can reconstruct the impulse response from the echoes, which is required to be able to reconstruct the 3D layout of a scene from the echoes.

claim: Kuc (1997) showed a bio-mimetic sonar device to be capable of detecting which side of a coin was up using very simple echo templates.
source: Kuc (1997) showed a bio-mimetic sonar device to be capable of detecting which side of a coin was up using very simple echo templates.

claim: A custom ensonification device consisting of 31 Knowles FG series microphones and a Senscomp Series 7000 ultrasonic speaker was used.
source: A custom ensonification device consisting of 31 Knowles FG series microphones (Steckel and Peremans, 2012) and a Senscomp (http://www.senscomp.com/ultrasonic-sensors/series-7000-sensors.php) Series 7000 ultrasonic speaker was used (see Figure 2).

claim: The speaker produces about 106 dBspl at 50 kHz and 1 meter distance.
source: The speaker produces about 106 d⁢Bs⁢p⁢l at 50 kHz and 1 meter distance.

claim: The device was mounted on a pan tilt system allowing rotation from −150 to 150 degrees in azimuth and from −25 to 40 degrees in elevation.
source: The device was mounted on a pan tilt system (PTU-E46, FLIR, Goleta, CA) allowing us to rotate the device from −150 to 150 degrees in azimuth and from −25 to 40 degrees in elevation.
evidence: Description of the experimental apparatus

claim: The pan tilt system moved the ensonification device through the full extent of its mechanical range in 31 steps of 10 degrees in azimuth and 7 steps of 10.8 degrees in elevation.

source: The positional error of the pan tilt system is less than 0.1 degrees.

source: A hyperbolic frequency modulated pulse sweeping from 100 to 40 kHz in 1 ms was emitted.

source: The recording of the echoes was started at the onset of the emission and ends 34 ms later.

source: The sampling rate was 219 kSamples/s.

source: Data was collected at three different sites (see Figure 3).

claim: Twelve positions in St. Andrews Park (Bristol, UK) were selected for ensonification.
source: First, twelve positions in St. Andrews Park (Bristol, UK, 51:27:15.772N, 2:36:52.996W) were selected for ensonification.
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: Four open, four semi-cluttered and four cluttered locations were selected at St. Andrews Park.
source: To ensure the data represented different densities of clutter bats might operate in, four open, four semi-cluttered and four cluttered locations were selected.
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: The data collected at St. Andrews Park consisted of 7812 echo trains at each of the 31 microphones.
source: The data collected at St. Andrews Park consisted of 7812 (12 positions × 217 directions × 3 repeats) echo trains at each of the 31 microphones.
evidence: Description of the data collected

claim: Data was collected in a park in Midreshet Ben Gurion, Israel at 50 positions along a straight line spaced 20 cm apart.
source: Second, data was collected in a park in Midreshet Ben Gurion, Israel (30:50:53.318N, 34:46:54.174E). At this site, bats use an artificial corridor lined with boulders as part of their commuting route. In this corridor, the ensonification device was placed at 50 positions along a straight line spaced 20 cm apart.
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: The Israel site data consisted of 32,550 echo trains at each of the 31 microphones.
source: At each of the 50 positions, three measurements for each of the 217 directions were collected yielding 32,550 echo trains (50 positions × 217 directions × 3 repeats) at each of the 31 microphones.
evidence: Description of the data collected

claim: Data was collected at Royal Fort Gardens (Bristol, UK) at 40 positions spaced 25 cm apart along a 10 meter line.
source: Finally, data was collected at Royal Fort Gardens (Bristol, UK, 51:27:26.417N, 2:36:4.619W). At this third site, 40 positions spaced 25 cm apart along a 10 meter line were sampled yielding 26,040 echo trains (40 positions × 217 directions × 3 repeats) at each of the 31 microphones.
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: In total, 66,402 echo trains for each of the 31 microphones were used in this paper, resulting in a data set consisting of a total of 2,058,462 echo trains.
source: In total, 66,402 echo trains for each of the 31 microphones were used in this paper, resulting in a data set consisting of a total of 2,058,462 echo trains.
evidence: Summary of the total data collected

claim: All echo trains were individually filtered using a model of the bats' auditory periphery similar to the one proposed by Wiegrebe (2008).
source: All 2,058,462 echo trains (217 directions × 3 repeats × 31 microphones × 102 positions) were individually filtered using a model of the bats' auditory periphery similar to the one proposed by Wiegrebe (2008) to simulate the peripheral hearing system of the bat Phyllostomus discolor.
evidence: Description of the data processing method

claim: The model consists of a Gammatone filterbank with central frequencies ranging from 30 kHz to 100 kHz in steps of 5 kHz.
source: In brief, the model consists of a Gammatone filterbank with central frequencies ranging from 30 kHz to 100 kHz in steps of 5 kHz.
evidence: Description of the auditory model used

claim: The resulting virtual beamwidth of the ensonification device has a 3 dB opening angle of 20 degrees at 55 kHz.
source: Using the theoretical beam directionality of the Senscomp ultrasonic emitter, we estimated the resulting beamwidth employed in this paper to have a 3 dB opening angle of 20 degrees at 55 kHz.
evidence: Calculated from the theoretical beam directionality

claim: For the Open environments, the probability of correct classification was very low (i.e. Pc∼0).
source: For the Open environments, the probability of correct classification was very low (i.e. Pc∼0).

source: In the Royal Fort Gardens data set, we found catchment distances up to 2.5 meter.

source: Across both data sets the average catchment distance was 0.89 meter (sd: 0.61), see Figure 10a.

source: A Wilcoxon rank sum test confirmed that the linear catchment distances for the Israel data were larger than for the Royal Fort Gardens data (Z=52.3,p≪0.01).

claim: The templates can be reliably classified, even using a system with a dynamic range smaller than a bat's.

claim: Templates collected in Open habitats could not be classified due to lacking systematic variation.
source: Hence, lacking systematic variation, templates collected in Open habitats could not be classified.

claim: Steckel and Peremans (2013) found that displacing a robot by about 14 cm or 20 degrees resulted in leaving the current template's catchment area.
source: These authors collected sonar based templates in an office environment by driving around a robot equipped with a biomimetic sonar system. They found that displacing the robot by about 14 cm or 20 degrees resulted in leaving the current template's catchment area.

claim: Successful navigation seems to be possible with catchment areas that are smaller than those found in this paper.
source: In spite of these small catchment areas, they successfully derived a map of the office using the templates. Hence, successful navigation seems to be possible with catchment areas that are smaller than those found in this paper.
